title: DungeonQuest - Let's Play
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4r4Fv5i5zCI

Daniel (@dungeondive) sets up the 1987 Games Workshop edition of DungeonQuest for a two-hero playthrough, joking that a let's play of a thirty-year-old game is the surest route to new subscribers. An elf and a barbarian (the latter a Warhammer Quest mini he painted himself, at roughly eight hours a figure) draw their rings, set the 26-turn sun track, and enter Dragonfire Castle knowing the rulebook puts survival at about 15%.

The barbarian's game is brief and instructive. His first tile is a rotating room that seals off his route, his second is a cave-in, and a passage down to the catacombs looks like salvation until he surfaces two cards later directly onto a trap tile. The trap card is another cave-in. He names a number, rolls it, and dies.

The elf fares better through what Daniel calls the craziest corridor of all time: portcullis after portcullis slamming shut behind him. He dodges two vampires, watches a death warrior and a mountain troll both flee, wrestles a ghoul and finishes it with arrows, finds ten gold, discovers a secret door, and then loses his torch two rooms from the exit. He relights it and escapes with his ten coins, the treasure chamber never glimpsed.

Daniel forgets to move the sun tracker more than once and invites viewers to count. He closes by defending the game as a perfect marriage of theme and press-your-luck mechanism, and admits he has never played the Fantasy Flight edition.

----

The elf escaped with ten gold and the barbarian died to a cave-in inside four turns. Is that randomness what makes DungeonQuest work, or what keeps it off your table?
